contents.title: The September BoJ meeting: what the Bank of Japan changed and how 10-year JGB yields reacted
contents.body:
## The September BoJ meeting: what was priced, what was new

I spent most of the week before the September meeting staring at the same question every rates strategist was asking: how much of this was already in the curve? My honest answer, as of the close on 17 September 2026, was most of it. The hike was roughly 85% priced by 17 September 2026, so the 9 bp rise in the 10-year yield on 18 September 2026 reflects guidance, not the move itself. That distinction matters more than the headline number, and it is the thing I want to unpack here.

Let me be careful about what I mean by priced. Overnight index swaps had been leaning toward a move for weeks, and the tone from the BoJ's communications had shifted just enough that the residual uncertainty was about timing and language, not direction. When the announcement came, the statement itself was almost anticlimactic. The vote was not unanimous, which I read as a signal that the board is still uncomfortable with the pace rather than the destination. The Governor's press conference then did the heavier lifting, and that is where the real information content sat.

## What the statement said, and what it did not

The statement language was, as usual, carefully hedged. It noted that underlying inflation was moving toward target in a manner consistent with the bank's projections, but it also flagged that the outlook for global demand remained unusually uncertain. I want to stress that second clause, because it is the part that gets stripped out in the wire copy. The bank is not declaring victory. It is saying that the conditions it set out in previous meetings have been met, and that it will continue to adjust the degree of monetary accommodation as needed. That is a conditional sentence, not a promise.

The Governor, in the press conference, was asked directly whether this was the start of a series. His answer, as I transcribed it, was that the bank does not pre-commit to a path and that every meeting will be judged on the data available at the time. He also said something that I think deserves more attention than it received: that the bank is paying close attention to the functioning of the JGB market, particularly at the longer end. That is not a throwaway line. It is a signal that the bank is aware that its own balance sheet and the shape of the curve are now intertwined in ways that make the exit harder than the entry.

## What the market did, and what it told us

The market reaction was instructive precisely because it was so contained. The 10-year JGB yield rose 9 bp on 18 September 2026, which is a move, but not a dramatic one given the context. The 2-year yield moved more, which is consistent with a repricing of the near-term policy path rather than a reassessment of the terminal rate. The curve flattened slightly, which is what you would expect if the market believes the bank is serious about normalising but also believes it will stop well short of anything that could be called restrictive.

What I found more interesting was the lack of follow-through in the following sessions. If the market had been genuinely surprised, we would have seen a sustained repricing, with the 10-year pushing through recent ranges and the yen strengthening sharply. That did not happen. Instead, the move faded, and By week's end the 10-year was back within a few basis points of where it started. That tells me the market's baseline was already close to the bank's baseline, and the meeting simply confirmed it.

I should also note the global backdrop. The Federal Reserve's own path was, at that point, still a source of uncertainty, and the ECB had been signalling caution. The BoJ is not operating in a vacuum, and the Governor was explicit that the bank is watching overseas developments. That is not just diplomatic language. It reflects a genuine constraint: if the Fed is cutting and the BoJ is hiking, the yen dynamics could become disorderly, and that is something the bank wants to avoid.

## The TSMC angle, and why I mention it

I want to bring in something that might seem tangential but is not. TSMC's capital expenditure plans for the coming year were released around the same time, and they pointed to continued strong demand for advanced semiconductors. For Japan, that matters because it feeds into the export outlook and, more importantly, into the investment cycle that the BoJ is hoping will sustain domestic demand. If TSMC is spending, Japanese equipment makers and materials suppliers benefit, and that shows up in the corporate surveys that the bank watches closely.

The reason I raise this is that the BoJ's decision was not made in a domestic vacuum. The bank's assessment of the output gap and the inflation outlook depends on external demand holding up. The Governor was asked about this and gave a careful answer, noting that while the semiconductor cycle was supportive, the bank was not relying on it. I read that as a hedge. The bank knows that if the global tech cycle turns, the case for further normalisation weakens considerably.

## What I am watching from here

The next few months will be about two things: wages and the curve. On wages, the shunto negotiations will start to come into focus, and the bank will be looking for evidence that last year's gains are being repeated. If they are, the case for another move strengthens. If they are not, the bank has cover to wait. On the curve, I am watching the long end. The bank's purchases have kept a lid on yields, but as it normalises, that lid will lift, and the question is whether the market can absorb the supply without a disorderly move.

I am also watching the communication. The bank has been careful to avoid surprising the market, and that has worked well. But as it moves further into normalisation, the room for gradualism shrinks. At some point, the bank will have to say something that is not fully priced. When that happens, the reaction will be larger than 9 bp. That is not a prediction, just an observation about how these cycles tend to end.

For now, the September meeting was a confirmation, not a turning point. The market got what it expected, and the bank got the space it wanted. That is a good outcome for both. But it does not tell us much about the next meeting, and anyone who claims otherwise is selling something.

contents.title: JGB benchmark yields, September 2026
contents.body:
## Daily closing levels for the 10-year JGB

The 10-year JGB yield closed at 2.05% on 17 September 2026, 2.14% on 18 September 2026 (+9 bp) and 2.19% on 22 September 2026, according to closing quotes published by the Japan Bond Trading Co. and cross-checked against data from the Ministry of Finance. The 18 September move represented the largest single-session increase in the benchmark tenor since the Bank of Japan exited its negative-rate policy in March 2024. Trading volumes on 18 September were reported at 2.4 trillion yen in the when-issued and on-the-run 10-year sector, compared with a 30-day average of 1.8 trillion yen. The 22 September close extended the rise, with the yield touching an intraday high of 2.21% before settling at 2.19%. No unscheduled operations were announced by the Bank of Japan on either date.

## Shorter maturities and the 2-year note

The 2-year yield rose 12 bp to 1.31% on 18 September 2026, according to data from the Japan Securities Dealers Association. That level was the highest for the 2-year tenor since July 2008. The 5-year yield closed at 1.72% on 18 September, up 10 bp from the prior session, while the 20-year yield closed at 2.58%, up 7 bp. The spread between the 2-year and 10-year yields narrowed to 83 bp on 18 September from 86 bp on 17 September. The Ministry of Finance's auction of 2-year notes on 17 September drew a bid-to-cover ratio of 3.12, compared with 3.45 at the previous auction in August. The next 2-year auction is scheduled for 15 October 2026.

## Bank of Japan operations and policy statements

The Bank of Japan conducted its regular outright purchase operations for 5-year to 10-year JGBs on 18 September 2026, offering to buy 600 billion yen at fixed-rate and variable-rate auctions. The operation was oversubscribed by a factor of 2.1. On 19 September 2026, the Bank of Japan released its quarterly outlook report, which stated that long-term interest rates would be allowed to "move more flexibly" in response to economic and price conditions. The report did not specify a target range for the 10-year yield. The next Monetary Policy Meeting is scheduled for 28-29 October 2026. Minutes from the September meeting, released on 25 September 2026, showed that seven members voted to raise the policy rate by 25 bp to 1.00%, while two members preferred to keep it at 0.75%.

## Domestic institutional flows and foreign activity

Japanese life insurers and pension funds reported net sales of 10-year JGBs totaling 1.2 trillion yen in the week ending 19 September 2026, according to weekly flow data from the Ministry of Finance. Foreign investors recorded net purchases of 480 billion yen in the same week, the third consecutive week of net buying. Regional banks reported net sales of 320 billion yen in the 5-year sector. The Tokyo Stock Exchange's JGB futures contract for December 2026 delivery settled at 146.32 on 22 September, down from 147.10 on 17 September. Open interest in the December contract stood at 112,000 lots on 22 September, compared with 108,000 lots on 17 September.

## Related market indicators and upcoming calendar

The Nikkei 225 index closed at 41,250 on 22 September 2026, down 0.8% from 17 September. The yen traded at 148.20 per dollar on 22 September, compared with 147.50 on 17 September. The Tokyo Stock Exchange's TOPIX bank index fell 1.2% over the same period. The Ministry of Finance is scheduled to auction 10-year JGBs on 1 October 2026 and 30-year JGBs on 8 October 2026. The Bank of Japan's next outright purchase operation for 10-year JGBs is scheduled for 25 September 2026. The Cabinet Office will release its monthly economic report on 30 September 2026. The Bank of Japan's next quarterly Tankan survey is due on 1 October 2026. All figures are as reported by the named sources and are subject to revision.

contents.title: BoJ monetary policy statement, 17–18 September 2026 meeting
contents.body:
The Bank of Japan released its monetary policy statement following the two-day meeting held on 17–18 September 2026. The statement was published on the Bank's website at 12:00 JST on 18 September 2026. According to the document, the Policy Board voted to raise the short-term policy rate by 25 basis points, from 0.75% to 1.00%, effective 19 September 2026. The vote was 7–2, with two members dissenting. The statement cited recent economic data and price developments as the basis for the decision. No further details on the dissenting opinions were provided in the statement.

## Policy rate decision

The policy rate increase from 0.75% to 1.00% marks the first change since the previous adjustment in July 2026. The Bank stated that the adjustment was necessary to maintain price stability and support sustainable growth. The statement noted that the economy has continued to recover moderately, with private consumption and business investment showing resilience. The Bank also mentioned that risks to the outlook include overseas economic conditions and fluctuations in financial markets. The decision was made after a thorough assessment of economic and financial conditions at the 17–18 September 2026 meeting.

## JGB purchase taper plan

The Bank confirmed that the taper plan for Japanese government bond (JGB) purchases was left unchanged. Under the existing plan, the Bank will reduce its monthly JGB purchases by approximately 400 billion yen every calendar quarter, aiming to bring monthly purchases down to about 3 trillion yen by the first quarter of 2027. The statement reiterated that the Bank will continue to monitor market conditions and adjust the pace if necessary. The taper plan was originally announced in July 2025 and has been maintained without modification since then. The Bank stated that the unchanged taper reflects its intention to avoid abrupt changes in the bond market.

## Economic outlook

The Bank's outlook for the Japanese economy remains cautiously optimistic. The statement projected that GDP growth for fiscal year 2026 would be around 1.2%, unchanged from the previous forecast in July. The consumer price index (CPI) inflation forecast for fiscal year 2026 was revised upward to 2.1% from 1.9%, reflecting recent increases in energy and food prices. The Bank noted that inflation expectations have been rising gradually. It also stated that it will continue to monitor wage growth and its impact on prices. The next Outlook Report will be published in October 2026.

## Market reaction

Following the release of the statement on 18 September 2026, the yen strengthened against the US dollar, moving from 145.20 to 143.80 within an hour. The Nikkei 225 index fell by 1.2% in afternoon trading. The yield on the 10-year JGB rose by 9 basis points to 2.14%. Analysts at several securities firms noted that the rate hike was largely expected, but the unchanged taper plan was seen as slightly dovish. Trading volume in JGB futures increased. The Bank's next monetary policy meeting is scheduled for 28–29 October 2026.

## Background

The Bank of Japan had maintained a negative interest rate policy until March 2024, when it raised the policy rate to 0.0–0.1%. Subsequent increases occurred in July 2024, January 2025, and July 2026, bringing the rate to 0.75% before the current meeting. The taper plan for JGB purchases was introduced in July 2025 as part of the Bank's efforts to normalize monetary policy. The Bank has stated that it will continue to adjust the degree of monetary accommodation as needed, with the aim of achieving the 2% inflation target in a sustainable manner. The statement on 18 September 2026 did not include any changes to the Bank's forward guidance, which remains that it will not hesitate to take further easing measures if necessary. The full text of the statement is available on the Bank of Japan's website.

contents.title: BoJ Meeting Recap: Market Reactions to Unexpected Signals
contents.body:
## Introduction

Speaking as an ex-central banker, I've learned to be wary of over-reading any single policy meeting. The Bank of Japan's gathering on 2026-09-30 was no exception. The statement itself was, in many ways, a masterclass in continuity. Yet the market's reaction was anything but continuous. In this newsletter, I will try to separate what the Bank actually said from what the market heard, and I will flag where my own interpretation remains uncertain.

The BoJ kept its policy rate unchanged at 0.5 percent, as most analysts expected. It also maintained its yield curve control framework, with the target range for 10-year JGB yields at plus or minus 0.5 percent around zero. The vote was 8-1, with one member dissenting in favor of a small hike. That dissent was not new; it has been a feature for several meetings. What was new, or at least seemed new to some, was the language in the outlook report.

## What the Bank Said

The key sentence, in my reading, was this: "The Bank will not hesitate to adjust the degree of monetary accommodation if underlying inflation dynamics warrant it." That is a conditional statement, not a commitment. It is also a phrase that has appeared in slightly different forms before. In April, the Bank said it would "consider adjusting" policy if needed. In July, it said it would "respond appropriately" to developments. The September wording is marginally more assertive, but it is still hedged by the word "if."

Governor Ueda's press conference reinforced the cautious tone. He noted that wage growth is broadening but remains uneven across small and medium-sized enterprises. He said the Bank is watching the yen's fluctuations but does not target the exchange rate. He also mentioned that the BoJ is in close contact with the government, which is standard. When asked directly about a possible move in October or December, he said the Bank does not pre-commit to a timeline. That is exactly what one would expect.

So, from a central-bank communication perspective, the message was: we are data-dependent, we see some progress, but we are not in a hurry. The dissent is a reminder that the board is not monolithic, but it is not a signal of imminent action.

## What the Market Did

Markets, however, often trade the path, not the level. Within minutes of the release, the yen strengthened from around 148.50 to 147.20 against the dollar. The 10-year JGB yield ticked up to 0.48 percent, still within the target band but near the upper end. The Nikkei 225 fell about 1.2 percent, with banks outperforming and exporters lagging. That pattern is consistent with a modest tightening of financial conditions, not a regime change.

What struck me was the speed and magnitude of the move in the yen. A 130-pip swing on a statement that was largely as expected suggests that positioning was stretched. Many investors had been short the yen, and the slightly more assertive language was enough to trigger a squeeze. I would not read this as a fundamental reassessment of the BoJ's reaction function. It is more likely a technical adjustment.

The JGB market was more measured. The 10-year yield rose, but the 20-year and 30-year yields were little changed. That tells me that the market does not expect a sustained tightening cycle. If it did, the long end would have sold off more. The curve steepened slightly, which is typical when the market prices a small chance of a near-term hike.

## The Global Context

It is impossible to analyze the BoJ in isolation. The Federal Reserve has been on hold since June, and the European Central Bank has signaled that it is done hiking for now. The Bank of England is in a similar position. In that context, the BoJ remains the odd one out, with negative real rates and a large balance sheet. But the gap is narrowing, slowly.

One factor that often gets overlooked is the behavior of Japanese institutional investors. Life insurers and pension funds have been increasing their allocations to domestic bonds as yields rise. That creates a natural demand for JGBs at higher yields, which may limit the upside in long-term rates. At the same time, Japanese banks have been reducing their foreign bond holdings, which reduces outward flow and supports the yen. These flows are gradual, but they matter.

Another factor is the semiconductor cycle. TSMC's recent guidance suggested a slower recovery in chip demand, which is relevant for Japan's exports. A weaker export outlook could make the BoJ more cautious, not less. So the market's hawkish interpretation of the statement may be overdone.

## My Take

I think the BoJ is in a difficult spot. Inflation is above target, but it is driven partly by cost-push factors that may fade. Wage growth is improving, but the Bank wants to see it sustained. The yen is weak, but the Bank does not want to be seen as targeting it. In that environment, the Bank will likely move slowly and communicate carefully.

For investors, the lesson is to distinguish between what the Bank says and what the market does. The September meeting did not signal a policy shift. It signaled a slightly higher probability of a future shift, which is not the same thing. I would not be surprised to see the yen give back some of its gains in the coming weeks, especially if U.S. yields rise again.

That said, I am not dogmatic. If the October services inflation print comes in hot, or if the winter wage negotiations show a stronger-than-expected outcome, the Bank could move earlier than I expect. I will be watching the data, not the headlines.

## Conclusion

The BoJ meeting on 2026-09-30 was a reminder that central-bank communication is an art, not a science. The Bank said what it needed to say: it is vigilant, it is flexible, but it is not pre-committed. The market heard a slightly more hawkish tone and reacted accordingly. As an ex-central-bank economist, I find that reaction understandable but probably excessive. The fundamentals have not changed enough to justify a sustained repricing. I will continue to monitor the data and the flows, and I will try to keep my own biases in check. After all, the market is often right, but not always in the way we expect.

contents.title: Powering a packaging plant in Penang
contents.body:
I spent last Tuesday morning in a meeting room in Bayan Lepas, staring at a single-line diagram that had been redrawn three times since breakfast. The subject was a new advanced packaging plant, and the question was simple enough to state and hard to answer: how do you feed it? I'll walk through the arithmetic here, because the numbers are the argument, and because I think the arithmetic is more interesting than the conclusion.

## The load, and why it is not just a number

The Phase 2 plant needs a 45 MW grid connection. That figure comes from the developer's own load schedule, which I have now read closely enough to have opinions about. It is not a constant. A packaging line is a collection of tools that cycle: etchers, deposition chambers, ovens, and the facility systems that keep them alive. The 45 MW is a coincident peak, the number you get when you assume the worst reasonable alignment of tool duty cycles on a hot afternoon in March.

What matters for the grid is not the peak alone but the shape around it. I asked for fifteen-minute interval data from the Phase 1 plant next door, which has been running since 2021. Its peak is lower, but its load factor is around 0.78, which is high for an industrial customer and tells you the plant is process-limited rather than batch-limited. If Phase 2 behaves the same way, its average draw will sit somewhere near 35 MW, and the difference between average and peak is what the network has to be able to absorb without voltage sag.

## What the grid can actually deliver

The transmission corridor into Bayan Lepas is fed from the main grid via 275 kV lines that terminate at a substation a few kilometres away. From there, 132 kV circuits distribute into the industrial parks. I pulled the most recent system adequacy report from the grid operator, and the southern corridor has headroom, but headroom is a seasonal thing. During the inter-monsoon months, when several large generators in the north go down for maintenance, the import capability into the island's southern tip tightens.

This is where the arithmetic gets uncomfortable. A 45 MW connection is not a 45 MW problem. If the plant's power factor at the point of connection is 0.95, the reactive power requirement is about 15 MVAr, and that has to come from somewhere: either the plant's own compensation or the network. If the plant installs capacitors to hold power factor near unity, the grid sees mostly real power, and the voltage support burden falls back on the transmission system. If it does not, the local 132 kV bus will sag every time a large motor starts.

I ran a rough short-circuit calculation with the fault level data I could get. At the proposed point of connection, the three-phase fault level is on the order of 1500 MVA. A 45 MW load is small against that, which is good news for voltage stability but bad news for protection coordination, because the plant's contribution to a fault is negligible and the utility's relays will not see it. That is a design detail, not a showstopper, but it is the kind of thing that adds months if it is discovered late.

## The generation side, and why I keep coming back to gas

Penang does not generate much of its own power. The island imports most of what it uses from the mainland, and the mainland's mix is dominated by combined-cycle gas and coal. I have written before that the marginal generator in Peninsular Malaysia is usually a gas turbine, and that is still true. So the emissions arithmetic for this plant is straightforward: 45 MW at a capacity factor of, say, 0.85 is about 335 GWh per year, and at a marginal emissions factor of roughly 0.45 tonnes of CO2 per MWh, that is about 150,000 tonnes per year. That is the number the sustainability team will have to defend, and it is why they keep asking me about power purchase agreements.

A dedicated PPA with a solar farm sounds attractive until you do the hourly matching. Solar in Penang produces at a capacity factor around 0.15 to 0.17, and it produces nothing at night, when the packaging lines run hardest. If you want 45 MW of firm capacity from solar plus storage, you are looking at a few hundred MW of panels and a battery that costs more than the plant's tool set. I am not saying it cannot be done; I am saying the arithmetic does not flatter anyone who claims it is cheap.

## What I would actually recommend

The boring answer is the right one. Connect to the grid, pay for a firm connection, and install enough on-site compensation to keep the power factor near unity. Then negotiate a PPA that matches the plant's actual load shape, not its peak. The 45 MW figure is a design constraint, not a procurement target, and treating it as the latter is how you end up with a battery you use four hours a day.

I would also push for interval metering at the point of connection from day one, and for a data-sharing agreement with the utility. The Phase 1 plant's data has been invaluable for this analysis, and I suspect the same will be true for Phase 2. Grid planning is a long game, and the more we know about how these plants actually behave, the better the next connection will be.

One last thing. The meeting on Tuesday ended with a decision to commission a detailed load flow study, which is the correct outcome. But I left with a nagging feeling that we are still planning these connections one plant at a time, when the real question is what happens when there are five of them. The southern corridor has headroom today. It will not have headroom forever, and the arithmetic that tells you when it runs out is the same arithmetic I have just walked through. I would rather do it now, in a meeting room, than later, in a blackout.

contents.title: How much power does an AI accelerator rack really draw?
contents.body:
## The question that keeps coming back

Every few weeks someone asks me the same thing after a seminar: how much power does one of those AI racks actually pull? The question sounds simple, but the answer depends on where you draw the boundary. Do you mean the chips alone, the whole server tray, or the rack as it appears on the data centre's electrical single-line diagram? I usually start with the chips, because that is where the primary data lives, and then work outward. It is the same method I teach in my load modelling course: begin with a nameplate, add the overheads you can defend, and state your assumptions out loud.

Let me be concrete. Take a current high-end accelerator, the kind that goes into training clusters. NVIDIA's published thermal design power for the H100 SXM is 700 watts. For the newer B200 it is around 1000 watts, and NVIDIA has said the GB200 Grace Blackwell superchip pairs two of those with a CPU. A GB200 compute tray, with two Blackwell GPUs and one Grace CPU, is rated at roughly 2700 watts. These are not my numbers; they come from the vendor's own datasheets and from the rack-level reference designs that NVIDIA publishes for its partners. When I cite figures in class, I make students find the primary source, because secondary reporting drifts.

## From one tray to a full rack

Now stack the trays. An NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 rack holds 18 compute trays, each with two GB200 superchips, so 36 Grace CPUs and 72 Blackwell GPUs in total. Eighteen trays at 2700 watts is 48.6 kilowatts of IT load before you add anything else. That is already a lot, but it is not the whole story. The rack also contains nine switch trays for the NVLink fabric, and those draw power too. NVIDIA's own documentation for the NVL72 puts the total rack power at about 120 kW under a sustained AI workload. A dense accelerator rack draws 120 kW at full load. That is the figure I use when I talk to utilities, because it is the one the vendor stands behind.

A single 120 kW rack is not a grid problem by itself. A hall of 100 such racks is 12 megawatts of IT load, and with cooling and losses you are at 14 to 17 megawatts. Unlike a factory that cycles, an AI training cluster can run at high utilisation for weeks, which means the utility cannot count on diversity to shave the peak. The fabs and the data centres are different loads, but they compete for the same transformers and the same skilled electricians. I mention these because energy systems professors are supposed to connect the chip to the grid, not just the chip to the benchmark.

If you take one figure away from this post, take 120 kW. From there you can scale: multiply by the number of racks, add cooling and losses, and you have a first-order estimate of the facility load. The arithmetic is not hard. contents.title: Cooling Load Dynamics in Southeast Asian Data Halls
contents.body:
## The humidity tax nobody budgets for

Last month I spent three days in a colocation facility on the outskirts of Singapore, watching a 4.2 MW data hall breathe. The operators were proud of their power usage effectiveness, a number they quote to prospective tenants the way a hotel quotes its star rating. But what struck me was not the PUE. It was the water.

In temperate climates, cooling a data hall is mostly a sensible-heat problem. You move air, you reject heat, you occasionally run a chiller. In the tropics, it is a latent-heat problem wearing a sensible-heat costume. Every cubic metre of outside air you admit carries water vapour, and that vapour must be condensed out before the air can do useful work. Condensation is not free. It is, in fact, the single largest hidden load in most Southeast Asian facilities I have audited.

Let me show you the arithmetic, because the arithmetic is where the argument lives.

## A worked example from a 4.2 MW hall

Take a hall with an IT load of 4.2 MW. Suppose the operators run a conventional chilled-water plant with a design PUE of 1.45. That gives a total facility load of 6.09 MW, of which 1.89 MW is cooling and losses. Now suppose they decide to economise by admitting outside air at 32 degrees Celsius and 80 percent relative humidity, which is a typical afternoon in Kuala Lumpur or Jakarta.

At those conditions, the air holds roughly 24 grams of water per kilogram of dry air. To bring it to a supply condition of 13 degrees Celsius and 95 percent relative humidity, you must reduce that to about 9 grams per kilogram. That is 15 grams of water condensed for every kilogram of dry air you push through the hall.

A 4.2 MW hall typically needs around 200 cubic metres per second of supply air, which is about 240 kilograms of dry air per second. Multiply by 15 grams and you get 3.6 kilograms of condensate per second. That is 3.6 litres per second, or about 311,000 litres per day. Three hundred and eleven cubic metres of water, every day, just to keep the air dry enough to cool the servers.

That water does not appear in the PUE. It appears in the water bill, and increasingly in the sustainability report, but it is invisible to the metric that the industry uses to compare facilities. This is a problem of measurement, not just of engineering.

## Why the standard playbook underperforms here

The standard playbook for efficient data centres was written in Oregon and Ireland. It assumes cool, dry outside air for much of the year. It assumes free cooling hours in the thousands. It assumes that water is cheap and abundant, or at least that its cost is second-order.

In Southeast Asia, none of those assumptions hold. Free cooling hours are close to zero in the lowlands. Water is a political resource, not just a utility. And the latent load is not a seasonal nuisance; it is the baseline.

I have seen designs imported wholesale from European reference architectures that specify indirect evaporative cooling, only to discover that the wet-bulb temperature in April is 28 degrees Celsius. Evaporative cooling cannot reach a supply temperature below the wet-bulb, so the design is dead on arrival. The fix is mechanical refrigeration, which means more electricity, which means a higher PUE, which means the facility looks worse on a scorecard that was never designed for this climate.

This is not a failure of engineering. It is a failure of benchmarking. We are comparing apples to durians and pretending the difference is a matter of skill.

## what the primary data really say

I want to tread carefully here, because there is a lot of hand-waving in this space. Let me cite what I can verify.

The International Energy Agency's 2024 report on data centres and networks estimates that data centres consumed about 460 terawatt-hours globally in 2022, roughly 1.5 percent of total electricity demand. That number is contested, and the IEA itself notes the uncertainty. But the direction is not contested: demand is rising, and it is rising fastest in regions where cooling is hardest.

Closer to home, Singapore's Energy Market Authority reported in its 2023 Singapore Energy Statistics that the information and communications sector accounted for about 7 percent of the country's electricity consumption, with data centres making up the bulk of that. The government has since imposed a pause on new data centre construction, not because of electricity alone, but because of water and land.

TSMC's 2023 sustainability report offers a useful comparison from a different industry. The company reported total water withdrawal of about 220 million cubic metres in 2022, with a recycling rate above 85 percent. That is a semiconductor fab, not a data hall, but the scale is instructive. A single large data centre campus in the tropics can withdraw tens of millions of litres per year for cooling, and unlike TSMC, most operators have not yet built the recycling infrastructure to match.

The Bank of Japan's 2024 Financial System Report included a chapter on climate-related risks to financial stability, noting that water stress in Southeast Asia poses a material risk to the region's industrial output. The BoJ is not an energy regulator, but its analysts are paying attention to the same physics I am describing.

## The path forward is unglamorous

The solutions are not exotic. They are, in fact, boring, which is why they are often overlooked.

First, stop admitting outside air when you do not need to. A sealed hall with a dedicated dehumidification loop can cut latent load by half or more. The trade-off is that you must handle internal moisture sources, which means better sealing and better monitoring. But the arithmetic favours sealing in almost every tropical case I have modelled.

Second, raise the supply temperature. Every degree you raise the chilled-water supply temperature reduces the lift on the compressor and improves the chiller's coefficient of performance. Modern servers can tolerate 27 degrees Celsius inlet air, and some can go higher. The ASHRAE TC 9.9 guidelines have been moving in this direction for a decade. The industry has been slow to follow.

Third, measure water separately from electricity. A PUE that ignores water is a half-truth. I would like to see a water usage effectiveness metric reported alongside PUE, with the same prominence. Some operators already do this. Most do not.

None of this is glamorous. It will not win a design award. But it will keep the lights on, the servers cool, and the water in the reservoir where it belongs. That seems like a reasonable trade to me.
